::: {.lead}
Yara has three takes of Pasha's meow. The best one still starts almost a
second late, has a low hum under it, ends with a click, and is quiet. The
programmer of *Rooftop Rescue* needs one clean file, named so that he finds
it at once. In lecture 13 you learned what a good take is. In this seminar
you **make** one: you record a short sound in the free **audio editor**
Audacity, clean it in a good order, and export it for a game. Every section
ends with a task, and at the end you have your own sound file, ready for a
game.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary audio-editor take sample-rate mono-stereo input-level trim-audio noise-reduction fade normalize clipping >}}

## 14.1 Record a sample in Audacity

Audacity runs on Windows, macOS and Linux and is free. Before Record, set it
up for a game sound.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 14.1 — The recording settings"}
1. **Project rate:** 48000 Hz (bottom left, or Audio Settings).
2. **Recording channels:** 1 (mono) for one source.
3. **Microphone:** choose it in the device toolbar; click the recording
   meter to watch the level.
4. **Level:** speak or make the sound; set the recording volume so that the
   peaks stay near −6 dB.
5. Record about **2 seconds of silence** first (the room tone), then three
   **takes** of the sound in one track.
:::

![From take to game file: the order of the edits.](images/edit-steps.png){#fig-steps width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 14.1 — Yara's session"}
1. Project rate 48000 Hz, 1 channel, the USB microphone.
2. The meter shows −6 dB when Pasha meows near the microphone.
3. She records: 2 s of room tone, then three meows with a pause between
   them. She saves the project as `pasha_meow.aup3`.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Pressing Record before checking the meter. If the first take clips, it is
lost. Watch the meter for a few seconds first, then record.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Record three takes"}
1. Open Audacity on the lab computer (or a free recorder app on your
   phone). Set 48000 Hz and mono.
2. Record 2 seconds of silence and three takes of one short sound: a cup
   on a table, a door, a clap, or your voice saying a game word ("Go!").
3. Save the project.

*Your result:* one project with room tone and three takes.
:::

## 14.2 Clean it: trim, noise reduction and fades

Now the take is cleaned in a good order: first cut, then remove the noise,
then make smooth ends (@fig-ba).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 14.2 — Three cleaning steps"}
1. **Trim:** select the parts before and after the best take and press
   Delete. Leave a few milliseconds of silence at the start.
2. **Noise reduction:** select a part of the room tone › Effect › Noise
   Reduction › **Get Noise Profile**; then select the whole take ›
   Noise Reduction again › OK. A steady hum or hiss gets much quieter.
3. **Fades:** select the last 0.1–0.2 s › **Fade Out**; if the start is
   hard, select the first few milliseconds › Fade In. Clicks at the ends
   disappear.
:::

![Pasha's meow before and after the edits.](images/before-after.png){#fig-ba width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 14.2 — Cleaning the meow"}
1. Trim: the meow started 0.9 s late; Yara deletes the silence, leaving
   0.05 s.
2. Noise Reduction: she takes the noise profile from the room tone and
   applies it to the take. The hum of the fridge is almost gone.
3. Fade Out: the last 0.2 s fades to silence, and the click at the end is
   gone.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/wave-editor.html" poster="sims/wave-editor.png" title="Wave Editor: clean up Pasha's meow" height="640" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Turning Noise Reduction up to the maximum. Too much reduction makes the
sound "watery" and robotic. Use a small amount, and listen.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Clean your best take"}
1. In **Wave Editor**, clean Pasha's meow in a good order.
2. In Audacity, clean your own best take: trim, Noise Reduction with the
   profile of your room tone, and a fade-out.

*Your result:* the four tasks of Wave Editor done, and your cleaned take.
:::

## 14.3 Normalize and export for the game

The clean take is still quiet. Raise it to a fixed level, then save it as
a game file (@fig-export).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 14.3 — Normalize and export"}
- **Normalize** (Effect › Normalize): raises the whole take so that the
  loudest peak reaches a chosen level, for example **−1 dB**. Do it after
  the cleaning, so that the noise is not raised too.
- **Export** (File › Export Audio): WAV, 16-bit, mono for a sound effect;
  OGG for music and long loops. Keep the project and the raw takes.
- **Name:** type_what_version, no spaces: `sfx_pasha_meow_01.wav`.
:::

![The format and the name tell the team everything.](images/export-names.png){#fig-export width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 14.3 — The meow is ready"}
1. The cleaned meow peaks at −14 dB. Normalize to −1 dB: now it peaks at
   −1 dB, with no clipping.
2. Export as WAV, 16-bit, mono: `sfx_pasha_meow_01.wav`, about 1 second,
   about 94 KB (48 000 × 2 bytes).
3. Yara puts it in the sound folder of the game and writes it in the sound
   list.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Using Amplify +20 dB instead of Normalize. 20 dB is 10 times louder: the
peaks pass 0 dB and clip. Normalize stops exactly at the level you choose.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Export your sample"}
1. Normalize your cleaned take to −1 dB.
2. Export it as WAV, 16-bit, mono, with a good name (sfx_…_01.wav).
3. Play the file in a media player. Does it start at once and end without a
   click?

*Your result:* one WAV file with a good name.
:::

## Case study: Clean Take

Yara edits the takes of *Rooftop Rescue* before she exports them. One meow
starts almost a second late; another take has a click at the end; one has a
hum under the whole sound; one is too quiet, with peaks near −14 dB; and one
is clipped. At the end, the clean meow needs a file name for the game's
sound folder. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses this story.

## Further reading

Audacity Manual, "Noise Reduction", "Normalize", "Fade In and Fade Out" and
"Exporting audio". Collins, *Game Sound* (2008), Chapter 5 (making sound
for games).

## Exercises

1. Which project rate and how many channels do you set for a sound effect?
2. Why do you record 2 seconds of room tone first?
3. Where should the peaks be while you record?
4. Write the three cleaning steps in order.
5. How does Noise Reduction learn which noise to remove?
6. Which edit removes a click at the end of a take?
7. Why do you normalize after the cleaning, not before?
8. Why is "Amplify +20 dB" risky?
9. Which format and settings do you export for a short sound effect?
10. Write a good name for the third version of a door sound.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. 48000 Hz and 1 channel (mono).
2. To get the noise profile for Noise Reduction.
3. Near −6 dB.
4. Trim, Noise Reduction, fades.
5. From a noise profile, taken from a part with only the noise (the room
   tone).
6. A short fade-out.
7. Normalizing first would make the noise and the clicks louder too.
8. It can push the peaks above 0 dB, so the sound clips.
9. WAV, 16-bit, mono.
10. `sfx_door_03.wav` (or `sfx_door_open_03.wav`).
:::
